newsitem.title: FRANCE: BoF's Gerard attacks German lack of understanding.
newsitem.headline: BoF's Gerard attacks German lack of understanding.

text.p: Bank of France monetary policy council member Jean-Pierre Gerard said in an interview in Le Monde on Thursday that while the current franc-mark rate posed no problems, German lack of understanding on monetary and exchange rate policy may make a change in the parity necessary.

Former president Valery Giscard d'Estaing was right to start a debate on the franc-mark rate when he called last week for a sharp depreciation in the franc, said Gerard, believed to be one of a minority of doves on the nine-member council.

"It is all the more necessary in that I believe that the Germans are not sufficiently aware of the problems which their monetary policy can have on the launch of the single currency," he was quoted as saying.
He said that while Germany was satisfied with the current dollar rate, for France the correct parity was around six francs per dollar, compared with 5.20 francs now.
One way to get the dollar higher would be to cut short-term interest rates in France and Germany. "Unfortunately we have little influence on German monetary policy.
"A second possibility, given that we cannot get a concerted reduction in rates, would be to modify the franc-mark parity. That is the reasoning of Monsieur Giscard d'Estaing.
"It is probably a less good solution since we are already overcompetitive compared to Germany, but German lack of understanding may make it necessary," he said.

Asked whether a devaluation of the franc would present a risk of deflation, he said, "Probably not. However a depreciation of the franc against the mark is not desirable, since this would increase market interest rates.
"However, there is an optimum balance to find between interest rates and exchange rates. This has not, as far as I am concerned, been reached today," he said.
"In other words, have we not paid very dearly to have long term interest rates which are among the lowest in the world given the weakness in the dollar?" he said.
He added that France could go a bit further in cutting interest rates, echoing comments made by council member Paul Marchelli on Tuesday.
Despite the calls for faster rate reductions, French economists still believe a majority of council members back continuing the Bank's traditionally cautious policy on rates.
